qa.answer:
The Group does not assume that demand will be linear through FY2031. However, over the long 
term, the Group believes the industry will continue to grow as semiconductors become increasingly 
important across a wider range of applications.  
 
The Group therefore believes that strategic investment through the industry cycle is key to 
enhancing its long-term competitive position. This provides the flexibility to capture opportunities, 
stay resilient, and continue progressing towards its FY2031 growth objectives. 
 
4. To what extent does the Group’s FY2031 growth plan depend on acquisitions, particularly 
in the Build-to-Print segment? What capabilities, technologies or geographic markets, if any, 
would management seek to acquire? 
The Group’s mid-term growth strategy focuses mainly on organic growth across three key priorities. 
The first is strengthening customer support through expanded operations and localised capabilities. 
The Group will strengthen its presence across key semiconductor markets to provide faster and 
more effective customer support. This includes expanding operations in China and Malaysia, where 
customers and the industry continue to grow, and building a stronger physical presence in Taiwan. 
The second is next-generation processing. The Group will invest in next-generation equipment and 
processes to enhance its capabilities in process-critical applications. 
The third is smart and secure manufacturing. The Group will increase the use of data-driven 
decision-making to improve operational effectiveness and support long-term innovation, while 
developing ISO 27001-aligned cybersecurity capabilities to strengthen its position as a trusted 
supplier of choice. 
The Group also remains open to acquisitions that can support these areas of its strategy, with its 
strong financial position providing the flexibility to act when suitable opportunities arise. 
 
B. Operations 
 
5. Decentralised operations depend on strong local decision-makers, and the share scheme 
appears designed to align managers’ interests with shareholders. With the COO and CFO 
retiring and the CEO stepping back to become Chairman, has responsibility shifted to the 
local management teams or become more concentrated at the top? 
The Group’s decentralised structure allows it to stay responsive to customers and provide quick 
local support with consistent, high-quality service. The Group takes a hands-on approach to 
management, working closely with teams on the ground to understand challenges and improve 
execution. 
The Five-Star Factory initiative helps bring this together by giving teams around the world a 
common framework for learning, sharing ideas and solving problems together. 
As part of its focus to build High Performance Teams, the Group continues to recruit and develop 
talent across all levels and locations, strengthening local support for customers worldwide.  
 
 

6. The Group will report a new segment, “Build-to-Print Precision Components”, starting in 
FY2027. Is the new segment principally a reclassification of the existing WFE parts business, 
or is it an expansion or reorganisation of the business? What has changed in the underlying 
activities, customer base, capabilities, strategic positioning or management structure? 
 
The change relates only to the segment descriptions and naming convention. It is intended to better 
reflect how the Group creates value for its customers, aligning segment reporting with its 
competitive positioning and strategic direction rather than the end-market served. There is no 
change to the Group’s underlying operations, management structure or reportable segments. 
 
7. How much of the Group’s core capabilities in consumable tooling are transferable to the 
manufacture of precision components for WFE, and what additional manufacturing 
capabilities, processes, technology or expertise does the Group need to develop to compete 
effectively in this market? 
The Group’s core capabilities are highly transferable across both business segments, as 
Consumable Tools and Build-to-Print parts require the same commitment to precision engineering, 
process control, quality, reliability and continuous improvement. The Group also benefits from a 
culture of sharing technical knowledge, lessons learned, and best practices across its operations, 
supported by the common framework of its Five-Star Factory initiative.  
As parts become more complex and customer requirements more demanding, the Group continues 
to invest in its process, quality and engineering capabilities to remain a trusted supplier of choice. 
In FY2026, these investments included a new machine to improve machining quality and efficiency, 
as well as a physics-based programming technology that can increase material removal rates by 
10-30% for long-cycle parts. With its mid-term growth strategy, the Group is also using data to 
improve operations and innovation, while strengthening cybersecurity in line with ISO 27001 
requirements. 
 
8. Where does MMUS sit in the WFE supply chain today, including whether it supplies directly 
to OEMs, contract manufacturers or other Tier 1 suppliers? Is MMUS itself qualified as a Tier 
1 supplier to any major WFE customers? How does the Group intend to leverage its current 
position to identify, qualify for and win larger WFE customers? 
MMUS mainly serves the Build-to-Print segment, supplying critical build-to-print precision 
components to WFE customers and other high-tech industries globally. Its parts are used in areas 
such as deposition and etch applications.  
As a Next Generation Supplier, its value lies in manufacturing difficult parts accurately, consistently 
and efficiently. The Group continues to engage customers to better understand and solve their 
problems, strengthen its engineering and manufacturing processes, and improve its factories 
through the Five-Star Factory initiative. This is increasingly important as semiconductor 
manufacturing becomes more complex and customers place greater emphasis on supplier 
capability and reliability. By consistently meeting these requirements, the Group believes the Build-
to-Print business can win more critical work over time. 
 
 

C. Financials 
 
9. Was the inventory write-off in FY2026 due to obsolescence (overproduction or unsaleable)? 
What is the typical average lead time before inventory goes obsolete? 
Inventory write-offs for FY2026 were S$73k, compared with S$166k in FY2025. Obsolescence risk 
varies by product, as customer requirements, part numbers and product programmes can change 
quickly. Under its Five-Star Factory initiative, the Group continues to improve the way it plans and 
manages inventory, while working to shorten lead times and deliver on time. 
 
10. Inventory stood at 6.5% of sales for FY2026 versus 4.8% of sales in the previous financial 
year. Is there a fixed threshold on this? 
With higher material costs and longer lead times, the Group built up inventory to fulfil confirmed 
backlog orders. 
While there is no fixed threshold for inventory, the Group remains disciplined in managing inventory 
levels and minimising obsolescence risk. This is especially important for the Consumable Tools 
segment, where customers’ requirements can change quickly as they seek to improve yields, cycle 
times and efficiency.
 
11. Can management provide a breakdown of the planned S$12.0 million of FY2027 capital 
expenditure between the Consumable Tools and Build-to-Print businesses? How much of 
the planned FY2027 capital expenditure is already supported by committed customer orders, 
contracts or capacity requirements, and how much is intended to build capacity ahead of 
anticipated demand? 
The Group does not disclose the breakdown the S$12.0 million investment by segment, or by 
committed versus anticipated demand. The investment is intended to support the three priority 
areas of its mid-term strategy: expanding operations and local capabilities, building next-generation 
processing capabilities, and advancing smart and secure manufacturing. 
The Group reviews its capital expenditure plans every six months to stay responsive to changing 
customer needs. This helps the Group invest with discipline and add capacity where it sees 
sustainable, long-term demand rather than reacting to short-term changes in the cycle. 
 
12. With FY2027 capital expenditure expected to increase significantly, can the Group fund its 
planned growth investments while maintaining the current 6-cent dividend? What factors 
does the Board consider in determining whether the 6-cent dividend can be sustained, and 
what gives the Board confidence that the higher investment programme will not come at the 
expense of shareholder distributions? 
For FY2026, total dividends represented a payout ratio of 52.4%. This exceeded the Group’s 
practice of distributing at least 40% of after-tax annual earnings, after considering financial 
performance, projected cash flow, capital requirements for business growth, and economic or other 
conditions. 
The Group remains focused on balancing long-term growth with sustainable shareholder returns. 
This means being thoughtful and disciplined about how capital is used, while ensuring that it does 
not limit good growth opportunities. The Group will continue this approach as it executes its mid-
term strategy, taking into consideration cash flow and investment needs.

Q2. Following two years of heavy capital investment, does management expect the 
company to generate consistently positive free cash flow moving forward?

qa.question:
The group has spent the past two years significantly expanding its manufacturing 
capabilities, product range, US waterfront footprint and European presence. Non-current 
assets increased from $49.2 million in FY2024 to $110.6 million in FY2026, with the carrying 
value of property, plant and equipment increasing from $34.2 million to $96.8 million over 
the same period.  
 
Management has indicated that the major investment programme is now largely complete. 
The increase in non-current assets appears to have been driven substantially by investments 
in the United States.  

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added)  
 
(i) 
Can management quantify the increase in manufacturing capacity at the 
Pasir Gudang facility, including the additional production capacity, 
capabilities and infrastructure added? How has the board assessed whether 
the investment has materially improved capacity, production efficiency and 
labour productivity, and what further investment, if any, is still required at 
the manufacturing facility? The carrying value of non-current assets in Malaysia 
stands at approximately $36.9 million, compared with $46.9 million of 
manufacturing facilities disclosed in FY20241. 
 
(ii) 
The group’s waterfront footprint expansion in the United States includes a marina 
in Newport, Rhode Island, waterfront apartments and an owners' club. How have 
these US assets performed since acquisition, and what financial and 
operating KPIs is the board using to assess whether the expansion is 
generating an adequate return on the capital invested? 
 
(iii) 
The group acquired the 100-foot Supermaxi, Palm Beach XI, for $12.1 million, 
including upgrades and modifications. What valuation and investment criteria 
did the board apply when approving the purchase, and what financial return 
or economic benefit was required to justify allocating $12.1 million to the 
yacht? 
 
 
1 The 2024 annual report states the following: The non-current assets, primarily the manufacturing facilities 
of $46,865,000 (2023: $42,944,000) are substantially located in Malaysia (2023: Malaysia)
qa.answer:
The substantial investments in the last two years are part of a strategic transformation 
across all aspects of the Group’s business, from manufacturing, marketing and customer 
service. Together, they have laid a strong foundation for future growth.  
The healthy sales orders recorded year-to-date in FY2027 are some of the first fruits of this 
combined strategy and underscore its potential in the years ahead. The Group expects 
operational cash generation and free cash flow to improve, mainly due to a stronger sales 
pipeline and moderation of capital expenditure requirements.  
The growth in cash flow will be partially offset by debt repayment obligations, as a portion 
of the capital expenditure was financed through third-party borrowings, as well as working 
capital movements due to yacht construction and delivery schedules. Nevertheless, 
management believes the Group is well-positioned to generate positive free cash flow on 
a sustainable basis over the medium term while progressively reducing leverage. 
 
Q3. How will the management allocate the resulting free cash flow among further 
expansion, acquisitions, debt reduction, dividend, inventory boats, share buyback (if 
any), etc.?  
Management’s near-term priority is to strengthen the balance sheet through servicing and 
gradually paying down debt incurred to fund the recent capital investments, while 
ensuring adequate working capital for the business.  
Beyond this, free cash flow will be allocated in a disciplined manner between organic 
growth opportunities and rewarding shareholders with dividends. There are no immediate 
plans for share buybacks. Management's objective is to deploy capital to the 
opportunities that generate the highest long-term returns for shareholders while 
maintaining operational and financial flexibility.  
 
Q4. What is the management target for ROE & ROIC over the next three years? 
Our forward guidance, as we have done for many years, has been to provide insight into 
the net order book and the number of boats contracted, which provide visibility on revenue 
and expected performance in the coming year. We will continue to provide these key 
indicators and update where there are material changes. As part of a broader review, we 
will consider, if appropriate, disclosure of other key metrics. 
 
 

 
 
3 
 
 
Q5. While we appreciate the past years' financial performance, how does the 
management balance ongoing growth with heightened vigilance toward potential 
market contractions that could impact operational stability and staffing levels?  
Management remains optimistic about the long-term prospects of the luxury yacht 
market but also recognises that market conditions can fluctuate, especially in view of the 
evolving tariff situation in the USA, conflicts in the Middle East and geopolitical and 
macro-economic uncertainties.  
Accordingly, management adopts a disciplined approach to growth, ensuring that 
investment plans, production schedules and cost structures remain aligned with 
demand. Even after the substantial capital expenditure in the last two years, management 
maintains a prudent balance sheet, adequate liquidity and close oversight of working 
capital. Importantly, management views its highly skilled workforce as a strategic asset 
and seeks to balance operational flexibility with the retention of critical capabilities. This 
approach enables the Group to pursue growth opportunities while maintaining resilience 
through market cycles. 
 
Q6. Has management assessed the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of utilising MAS 
GEMS funding to co-sponsor market-making activities and enhance our equity 
liquidity? 
Management is aware of the MAS Grant for Equity Market Singapore ("GEMS") scheme and 
periodically reviews initiatives that may enhance the Company's market visibility and 
share liquidity. 
Historically, the GEMS scheme has been focused primarily on supporting Singapore's 
equity capital markets through incentives for IPOs, secondary listings, RTOs and the 
development of equity research coverage. 
More recently, MAS has expanded the scope of GEMS to include support for market-
making activities in selected SGX-listed stocks to improve trading liquidity and price 
discovery. 
The Company is also actively exploring other incentive schemes related to the capital 
market, including the MAS-SGX Value Unlock initiative.  
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
4 
 
 
Q7. In line with SGX RegCo's guidance encouraging measurable forward disclosures 
rather than qualitative outlooks, does the Board plan to provide range-bound 
operational targets-such as projected hull deliveries, yard slot utilisation, or gross 
margin bands-to give shareholders clearer earnings visibility; if not, what key 
constraints prevent this?  
(Please refer to the Group’s response to Q4). 
 
Q8. I would like to propose a suggestion that the company provides a video-tour of its US 
facilities in Stuart and Newport, including the refurnished Owners' Club and the 11 
new waterfront apartments, as well as the revamped factory layout in Pasir Gudang, 
Johor Bahru, Malaysia (if completed).  
We plan to present a video at the AGM.  
 
Q9. What annual revenue can the expanded Pasir Gudang factory sustainably support? 
The objective of the recent expansion at Pasir Gudang is not just to increase production 
volume, but also to remove bottlenecks, improve workflow, enhance manufacturing 
flexibility and create the capacity to support a wider range of models and future growth 
opportunities. 
The Company currently offers a broad range of boat models of different sizes, 
specifications and selling prices, and the production mix can vary significantly from year 
to year. Revenue is also affected by the stage of completion of individual boats and the 
timing of deliveries. 
Accordingly, the sustainable revenue capacity of the expanded factory will depend on the 
model mix, production efficiency, labour availability and utilisation of the expanded 
facilities. More importantly, the expansion provides the Group with the flexibility and 
capacity to progressively increase production as demand grows. 
 
Q10. Why did new yacht orders fall from 33 to 18, and what is the latest order intake since 
30 June?  
In FY2026, the luxury yacht market was impacted by the evolving tariff situation in the 
USA, as well as the war in Iran, which dampened consumer sentiment. Despite the 
challenging operating environment, the Group achieved an all-time high revenue of 
S$173.2 million.  
Management wishes to emphasise that the Group's product portfolio comprises 
approximately 19 yacht models across the Grand Banks, Eastbay and Palm Beach brands, 

 
 
5 
 
ranging from around 42 feet to over 100 feet in length. Given the significant differences in 
vessel size, specifications and selling prices, a single larger yacht can generate 
substantially more revenue and profit than several smaller yachts combined. 
Accordingly, management focuses not only on the number of yachts ordered, but more 
importantly on the value, mix and quality of those orders. These factors are more relevant 
indicators of future revenue, profitability, cash generation and long-term shareholder 
value than unit volumes alone. 
Please refer to the Group’s response to Q1 for the latest order intake since 30 June 2026. 
 
Q11. Why did completed stock boat inventory increase from $5.9m to $27.7m? 
The increase reflects a higher number of trade-in boat transactions during FY2026. 
As part of the sales process, the Group periodically accepts customers' existing boats as 
trade-ins. During FY2026, the number and value of such trade-in transactions rose, 
resulting in a higher inventory of boats being held at year-end. 
These inventories are directly linked to new yacht sales activity, and increased levels of 
trade-in boats indicate that more customers are trading up to a larger Grand Banks or Palm 
Beach yacht, which is a positive indicator for the business. 
 
Q12. How much capex will be needed in FY2027 and FY2028, split between maintenance 
and growth?  
With the major expansion programme now substantially completed, management 
currently expects productivity-related capital expenditure to be substantially lower.  
 
Q13. Recurring services: Can service, berthing, storage and brokerage grow without 
proportionately large new investments? What does management expect to see in 
these revenue growth?  
Our core business is in the manufacturing and sales of yachts. Service, berthing and 
brokerage are ancillary activities which can be expected to grow in tandem with the core 
business. These activities do contribute to the overall business and build the Group’s 
brand value, customer experience and overall reputation. 
 
Q14. What financial returns have been achieved from the Newport, Stuart and other 
waterfront investments?  
Over the last two years, Grand Banks has built up a footprint which combines 
manufacturing operations in Malaysia, a flagship marina in Newport as well as service 
centres in other parts of the USA. This footprint is part of a combined strategy to increase 

 
 
6 
 
the value proposition of the Group, which does not see the waterfront assets as 
standalone investments to be assessed purely on their individual financial returns.  
 
Q15. What is the expected return on the European investment? 
Having established a transformation of the company with a factory-direct model, which 
has proven very successful, Grand Banks is now widening its market reach in Europe. The 
luxury boating community in Europe remains vibrant, especially in the Mediterranean 
region. 
The Group has established an asset-light facility in Sanremo in northwest Italy as part of 
its strategy to grow its presence in Europe and capture sales opportunities there.  
It is too early to project expected returns on the European investment. 
 
Q16. What sustainable net profit margin does management expect at normal production 
utilisation?  
(Please refer to the Group’s  response to Q9). 
 
Q17. Over the past decade, management has transformed Grand Banks from a company 
with annual revenue of approximately S$59 million into one generating S$173 million.

Q24. How is management evaluating underlying end-market demand across North 
America and Europe amid elevated global interest rates and macroeconomic

without resorting to price discounting or margin-eroding sales incentives?  
Management continuously monitors underlying demand trends across the Group’s key 
markets in North America and Europe through multiple indicators, including industry 
updates, customer enquiries, boat show activities, order conversion rates, financing 
conditions and broader economic developments. While elevated interest rates and 
macroeconomic uncertainty may influence purchasing decisions and extend sales 
cycles, we believe demand for well-differentiated products in the premium luxury 
segment remains fundamentally supported by long-term wealth creation, lifestyle trends 
and customer confidence in established brands. 
The investment in Palm Beach XI, which is part of a key pillar to sustain technology and 
product innovation. The Group’s proprietary V-Warp® Technology, advanced composite 
construction techniques and emphasis on fuel efficiency, performance and range provide 
a clear point of differentiation in the marketplace. Management believes customers are 
increasingly attracted to products that offer superior ownership economics, safety, 
comfort and performance rather than simply the lowest purchase price. 
At the same time, the Group is embarking on a strong marketing push for our Grand Banks 
and Palm Beach brands. This is part of our strategy to elevate brand awareness and 
customer engagement. In this regard, Palm Beach XI serves as a powerful global 
marketing and brand-building platform. Beyond enhancing brand visibility, the iconic 
vessel showcases the technology, engineering capabilities and performance DNA that 
underpin the Group’s yachts. Management believes this association with innovation, 
excellence and world-class sailing helps elevate brand recognition and strengthen 
customer interest across our product portfolio. 
In addition, management continues to focus on: 
- Strengthening customer engagement through boat shows, owner events and curated 
brand experiences;  
- Expanding its reach within existing and prospective customer segments through 
opening service offices in Europe and the West Coast of USA; 
- Enhancing the ownership experience through high levels of customer support, owner 
satisfaction and engagement supported by our US marinas, service centres and the 
new Newport RI Owners Club, along with our other factory direct sales and service 
locations in Europe, Australia and the West Coast of the USA;

- Leveraging 
the

responsiveness to customer requirements; and 
- Building long-term relationships that generate repeat purchases and owner referrals. 
Ultimately, our objective is to secure quality orders rather than merely increasing volume. 
We believe that sustained order growth is best achieved through technological leadership, 
product excellence, brand strength and customer experience. 
 
Q25. With the major investment phase largely complete, what specific operational

The primary objective of the investments made over the past two years was to remove

be on extracting returns from these investments.  
Specifically, we expect to achieve improvements in production efficiency and delivery 
schedules while increasing utilisation of our expanded facilities and manufacturing

The Board's priority is to ensure that the investments already made translate into 
sustainable, profitable growth and long-term shareholder value. 
 
Q26. When does management anticipate gross profit margins returning to 30%+ or higher

While 30%+ gross margins remain a desirable long-term outcome, it is important to note 
that this figure is a blended Group metric across multiple revenue streams. It includes not 
only include new yacht construction, but also trade-in/pre-owned boat sales, brokerage 
activities, service revenues and berthing revenues. Accordingly, the reported gross margin 
can vary significantly depending on the mix of these revenue streams in any given year. 
With the major investment phase largely completed, management is focused on 
increasing utilisation of our expanded facilities, improving productivity, maintaining

Q27. Can management quantify the increase in manufacturing capacity at the Pasir 
Gudang facility, including the additional production capacity, capabilities and

increased total manufacturing footprint by about 25%. The Group has also introduced 
advanced manufacturing capability, new materials, robotics, engineering laboratories 
and testing facilities. 
Due to the wide range of models offered, it is not meaningful to measure the Group’s

Instead of boat count, management focuses on improvements in throughput, workflow 
efficiency, production flexibility, quality, labour productivity and delivery performance. 
We are already seeing benefits in these areas, although the full benefits will continue to 
be realised as production volumes increase and the facilities become more fully utilised. 
This major expansion phase is largely complete. Future capital expenditure will be

Q29. The group acquired the 100-foot Supermaxi, Palm Beach XI, for $12.1 million, 
including upgrades and modifications. What valuation and investment criteria did 
the board apply when approving the purchase, and what financial return or economic 
benefit was required to justify allocating $12.1 million to the yacht?  
The Board regards Palm Beach XI as a strategic investment in brand development, 
technology leadership and customer engagement, rather than as a standalone financial 
investment expected to generate a specific short-term financial return. 
It is one of the world's most recognised supermaxi racing yachts and provides a unique 
global platform to showcase the Palm Beach brand, its engineering expertise, 
performance credentials and innovation capabilities to a highly relevant audience of 
existing and prospective yacht owners. 
In assessing the investment, the Board considered a range of factors, including the 
acquisition cost relative to the yacht's market value and replacement cost, the condition 

 
 
12 
 
and pedigree of the yacht, the expected useful life of the asset, its global media exposure 
potential and its ability to strengthen the positioning of the Grand Banks and Palm Beach 
brands in key markets. 
Beyond marketing and customer experience, Palm Beach XI also serves as a technology 
and innovation platform. The extreme demands of supermaxi racing provide valuable 
opportunities to develop, test and evaluate advanced materials, construction techniques, 
performance optimisation and engineering solutions. Where appropriate, such 
technologies and applications will be incorporated into future models, supporting 
ongoing product development and reinforcing the Group’s reputation for innovation. 
Management believes that competing successfully at the highest level of offshore yacht 
racing such as the Rolex Sydney Hobart Yacht Race enhances brand credibility and 
showcases the engineering principles, craftsmanship and performance DNA that 
underpin our production yachts. 
Accordingly, the Board evaluates the success of the investment through a combination of 
financial and strategic measures, including brand exposure, media coverage, customer 
engagement, lead generation, owner events, technology development opportunities, 
relationship-building activities and the longer-term contribution to yacht sales and 
shareholder value. 
 
Q30. Can the board explain the strong need/impetus, if any, for allowing independent 
directors to participate in the ESOS 2026, particularly where options may be granted 
at a discount of up to 20% and the remuneration committee, comprising these same 
independent directors, is responsible for administering the scheme?  
The Board believes that it is appropriate to include Non-Executive Directors, including 
Independent Directors, within the scope of the ESOS 2026. 
Although Independent Directors are not involved in the day-to-day management of the 
Group, they play an important role in contributing their experience, expertise, judgement, 
industry knowledge and governance oversight to support the Group's long-term success. 
The Board recognises that such contributions may not always be appropriately rewarded 
through directors' fees or other forms of cash payment, as Independent Directors often 
provide strategic guidance or other value that is difficult to quantify in monetary terms. 
The inclusion of Independent Directors in the ESOS 2026 therefore provides the Company 
with an additional mechanism to recognise their contributions, align their interests more 
closely with those of shareholders and assist the Company in attracting, retaining and 
motivating experienced and qualified directors. 
With respect to the concern regarding options which may be granted at a discount of up 
to 20%, whilst the ESOS 2026 provides flexibility for the Company  to do so, it does not 
necessarily mean that options will be granted at a discount as a matter of course. Any 

 
 
13 
 
grant will be considered by the Remuneration Committee on a case-by-case basis having 
regard to the circumstances at the time. 
The Board would also highlight that as stated in the Appendix to the Annual Report, the 
Company intends to grant only a nominal number of options under the ESOS 2026 to Non-
Executive Directors and Independent Directors. In addition, any director who has an 
interest in a proposed grant will abstain from all deliberations, recommendations and 
voting relating to that grant. These measures are intended to minimise any potential 
conflict of interest and ensure that the scheme is administered in accordance with good 
corporate governance practices. 
 
Q31. Have any independent directors indicated that they do not intend to participate in the 
ESOS 2026? Did the remuneration committee consider whether participation by 
independent directors is appropriate as a matter of principle, given the potential 
perception of a conflict between receiving equity incentives and maintaining 
independent oversight?  
No Independent Director has formally indicated that he or she will participate in or decline 
participation in the ESOS 2026.  
The Remuneration Committee and Board have considered the governance implications 
of allowing Independent Directors to participate and recognise that there can be opposing 
views on this issue. On one hand, equity participation will help align directors' interests 
with those of shareholders. On the other hand, some may view that equity incentives 
could affect, or be perceived to affect, a director's independence. 
After considering these factors, the Board decided it was appropriate to retain the 
flexibility to include Independent Directors as eligible participants, and not exclude their 
participation entirely. However, the Remuneration Committee will carefully assess any 
future grants of options to any Independent Director, having regard to corporate 
governance considerations, independence requirements and shareholder interests. 
Importantly, any Independent Director being considered for an award would abstain from 
all discussions and decisions relating to his or her own participation. No director would 
be involved in determining his or her own award. 
Accordingly, the Board believes that the appropriate safeguard against the risk of potential 
conflict between receiving equity incentives and maintaining independent oversight is 
through strict governance controls and careful case-by-case consideration should such a 
situation arise in the future, rather than excluding participation of Independent Directors 
from the ESOS 2026 entirely. 
 
 

 
 
14 
 
 
Q32. Can the board and the company secretary explain specifically how the failure to 
obtain the requisite independent shareholder approval occurred? Was the director 
himself unaware of the need for approval by independent shareholders when he 
accepted and subsequently exercised the options?  
The issue arose from an oversight. Upon discovery, the Company sought professional 
advice and will seek ratification from independent shareholders at the upcoming AGM. 
 
Q33. Following this realisation, what improvements have been made to the company's 
internal processes for ESOS 2026 and PSP 2026 to prevent a similar failure, including 
the roles of the company secretary, remuneration committee, board and external 
advisers? Has the board independently assessed whether its existing governance 
processes and directors' understanding of the relevant SGX requirements are 
sufficiently robust?  
Following the discovery of the oversight, the Board has introduced additional controls for 
both the ESOS 2026 and PSP 2026, including engaging external legal and professional 
advisers, to confirm that all shareholder approval and regulatory requirements have been 
satisfied before any award is granted. 
In particular, proposed awards involving directors or other persons subject to special 
approval requirements will be specifically reviewed to ensure that the necessary 
approvals are obtained before implementation. 
These controls are in addition to the existing formal review process involving the Company 
Secretary and the Remuneration Committee.   
The Board has also reinforced the role of the Company Secretary and external advisers in 
advising on compliance with the SGX Listing Rules, the Companies Act and the rules of 
the PSP 2026 and ESOS 2026. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
15 
 
 
Q34. If independent shareholders do not approve the ratification, what are the legal, 
financial and accounting consequences for the company, the directors and the 
recipient of the options?  
If independent shareholders do not approve the ratification, the Company will seek advice 
from its lawyers and auditors on the legal and accounting implications. 
The Company firmly believes that all directors provide invaluable contributions and 
should not be excluded from the PSP 2026 and ESOS 2026 schemes. Hence, the 
proposed schemes provide for all directors (including those who are controlling 
shareholders and/or their associates) to participate subject to independent shareholders' 
specific approval. These resolutions will be voted on by independent shareholders at the 
coming AGM.
